idiom_name: abstract port interface + adapter class; vendor headers only in the .cpp
implementation_notes: The domain declares a pure abstract port (virtual ~OrderPort() = default; virtual Receipt place_order(const Order&) = 0;) and the layer supplies an adapter whose .cpp is the only file including the vendor header; models cross the seam as local aggregates converted by free functions (Order to_domain(const legacy::order&)). std::unique_ptr owns the adapter and the vendor library is linked into the layer target alone. What replaces the classic facade/translator pair is the port plus these conversion functions; the fuller class hierarchy is still justified when several adapters implement one port or when the boundary must be injected for tests.
pitfalls: A vendor type in the port header (by value, or a forward-declared pointer handed to callers) silently re-couples the domain and defeats the firewall; keep vendor includes in the .cpp.
The adapter must own or outlive the vendor client: a raw pointer to a stack-allocated client is a classic dangling reference.
Vendor exceptions crossing the port break the local error vocabulary; catch at the seam and translate.

variants.name: Pimpl compilation firewall (vendor headers hidden entirely)
variants.idiom_name: one boundary class with pImpl; vendor headers live in the .cpp
variants.implementation_notes: When the upstream ships heavy, macro-laden or ABI-fragile headers, the whole layer collapses into one class with a pimpl: the public header declares only local types and a private struct impl*, while the .cpp includes the vendor headers, owns the vendor client and does both translation and transport. This is the classic C++ boundary-as-compilation-firewall form - it also keeps vendor macros and ABI out of your build - and it is justified precisely when header hygiene matters more than role separation. Because the class hides its implementation, tests substitute it through the port interface the class implements.
pitfalls: A raw impl* means hand-written destructor, copy constructor and assignment operator (or deleted copies) - otherwise double frees and shallow copies appear.
The pimpl hides vendor types but not vendor behaviour: error codes, retries and units still have to be translated explicitly inside the .cpp.
One class doing translation, transport and retry grows unwieldy; split translator functions out of the .cpp once the mapping gets large.

variants.name: Free mapping functions with injected translators (no class hierarchy)
variants.implementation_notes: When the boundary is a handful of small conversions, skip the port/adapter classes: write a pure function per upstream operation (Receipt place_order(const Order&, const Submit&)) that translates, calls and translates back, and inject as std::function only what genuinely varies (the client call, the clock, the retry policy). This keeps the layer testable with lambdas and makes each translation visible in one place; the class-based port is still justified when several adapters implement one contract or callers need a stable injectable type.
pitfalls: std::function copies and indirects on every call and hides the concrete type in diagnostics; template the mapper on the callable in hot paths.
A stored std::function capturing by reference dangles once the client it captured is gone - the failure surfaces far from the assignment.
Without a named port type callers can pass any callable, so the contract drifts; document or wrap the signature once more than one call site exists.
